rationale:
Evidence: all seven designs so far went off track in all 60 trials, with max_error at 0.060 to 0.066 m whatever the gain, speed, sensor span, mass or ki. Iteration 5 (ki 1.5) and iteration 6 (ki 1.0) reproduced iteration 3 almost exactly, so the integral term is not the binding limit. The 7-sensor, 0.06 m span in iteration 5 also matched iteration 3, so line loss at the array edge is not what ends the runs. The Evaluator's critique is right that the uniform 0.06 m departure may come from a fixed early departure, but I cannot change the start. Of the remaining levers, wheel_track has not been tested. It sets turn rate per unit wheel-command difference (turn rate = (wL - wR)/track), so it controls how much steering authority each unit of turn gives.

Decision: I keep the best-scoring layout (5 sensors at x -0.032 to +0.032 in 0.016 m steps, y 0.05, size 0.012, weights -1, -0.5, 0, 0.5, 1, mass 0.8, wheel_radius 0.03, body unchanged). I keep the controller from iteration 6 (kp 1.5, ki 1.0, kd 0.1, base_speed 1.0, last_direction), so the only change from the baseline is wheel_track 0.14 to 0.10. I reject the critique's kd 1.0 and mass 0.4 changes, because the sensor-edge derivative kick is large and no oscillation evidence supports them. I also reject the critique's suggestion to lower base_speed, since progress has risen with speed.

Expected result (hypothesis): if steering authority was the limit, max_error should fall below 0.061 and progress on the oval should rise above 0.17. If max_error stays at 0.061 to 0.066 with the same timing, the cause is not steering authority, and the next step is to test the start condition or accept the current best. A sharper turn response may raise steering_oscillation; if it exceeds about 0.25, the wheel_track change is too aggressive and the next step is 0.12.
